mcqs.question: A process's virtual pages 0-3 map to physical frames 40, 3, 812, and 41. What does this tell you about pages and frames?
options: This is invalid — pages must map to frames in the same numeric order
Pages (virtual) and frames (physical) are independent numbering spaces; a page can map to any frame regardless of its own number
The process must be experiencing a page fault on every access
Frames and pages must always be different sizes for this to work
mcqs.explanation: Pages and frames are separate spaces connected only by the page table; there's no requirement that frame numbers follow page order, and this scattering is completely normal. It doesn't imply constant page faults, and pages/frames must actually be the same size for the offset bits to carry over unchanged.

mcqs.question: What does a Page Table Entry (PTE) fundamentally record for one virtual page?
options: The full contents of that page
A list of every process that shares that page
The virtual address of the next page in the process
The physical frame that page currently occupies, plus status bits like valid/invalid and permissions
mcqs.explanation: A PTE stores the frame mapping and status bits (valid, permissions), not the page's actual data, a list of sharing processes, or a pointer to the next page.

mcqs.question: With 4 KB pages, virtual address 0x2050 maps to physical frame 3 via the page table. What is the physical address?
mcqs.explanation: Offset = 0x2050 & 0xFFF = 0x050; physical = (frame << 12) | offset = (3 << 12) | 0x050 = 0x3050. The physical address is neither the unchanged virtual address, the bare frame base, nor an address with the wrong offset added.

mcqs.question: Why does a flat, single-level page table become impractical on a 64-bit system with a 48-bit virtual address space?
options: 64-bit CPUs don't support page tables at all
Page table entries become larger than a physical frame on 64-bit systems
64-bit systems don't allow more than 4 GB of virtual memory per process
The number of entries needed (roughly 2^36 for 4 KB pages) would require tens of terabytes per process, for an address space that's mostly unused
mcqs.explanation: The entry count scales with the size of the addressable space, not how much of it is actually used, and at 48-bit address spaces that count is astronomically large — hence multi-level or inverted tables. 64-bit CPUs support paging fine, PTEs don't exceed frame size, and 64-bit address spaces are far larger than 4 GB.

mcqs.question: Why does a device needing DMA typically require physically contiguous memory, when the OS normally hands out virtually contiguous pages?
options: DMA hardware doesn't understand the page table abstraction and reads/writes raw physical addresses directly, so virtual contiguity guarantees nothing to it
DMA is actually unaffected by physical layout
Page tables automatically make all allocations physically contiguous
DMA only works with a single page at a time, so contiguity is irrelevant
mcqs.explanation: DMA hardware operates outside the CPU's virtual-memory translation, so it needs real physical contiguity for a multi-page transfer — virtual contiguity is irrelevant to it. Page tables don't guarantee physical contiguity, and DMA transfers commonly span more than one page.
